newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Greece veto overshadows EU meeting with Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greece veto overshadows EU meeting with Turkey.

text.p: Greece maintained its long-standing veto on a European Union aid package to Turkey on Tuesday, casting a shadow over the bloc's first high-level talks with Ankara since 1995.

At a meeting in which Turkey was told it could one day become an EU member and Greece and Turkey agreed a system for solving their disputes in the Aegean, the veto dashed hopes of Athens easing its hardline stance against its longtime rival.
Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said his country could not agree to unblock aid worth 375 million ecus ($424 million) until Turkey stopped threatening Greek sovereignty in the Aegean.
"We have repeatedly declared that we cannot accept Turkish behaviour vis a vis our sovereignty," he told a news conference.
Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said the move was disappointing.
"We have missed an historic opportunity," she told reporters after meeting EU foreign ministers.
The aid package has been promised to Ankara to help it meet the increased competition posed by the customs union which entered into force with the EU in January 1996.
Without it, Turkey has said it has felt little benefit from the deal.
EU officials had earlier expressed hope that Greece was about to change its mind about the aid, but Pangalos remained adamant.
He said Turkey had to "withdraw the threat of war" over Greek plans to extend its maritime borders and must turn to international law to solve disputes in the region.
"We will continue in this firm position until we have satisfaction from the Turkish side," he said.
Despite the veto, EU officials reported some progress in the bloc's often stormy relations with its predominantly Moslem southern neighbour.
Greece and Turkey formally agreed an approach to solving their differences in the Aegean, where they almost came to blows last year over some uninhabited islets.
They were each to appoint two non-governmental negotiators to submit a report in mid-June with recommendations for dealing with the situation.
EU-Turkish relations were strained earlier this year when mainly Christian Democratic politicians ruled out future Turkish membership of the EU because of cultural differences.
The bloc's foreign ministers, however, emphasised the official EU position that Turkey will be treated in the same manner as other applicants such as Poland and Hungary.
"The EU reaffirms Turkey's eligibility for EU membership," the ministers said in a statement.
But Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, sitting next to Ciller at the news conference, indicated Ankara's road would not be easy.
"This will be a tough job...and will take some time," he said.
